lessons.title: Local government and traditional authorities

objectives: Define local government and traditional authority
Name the main services of a council
Explain how citizens take part in local affairs
reviewNotes: Teacher to verify: titles (mayor, council, commune), the services of councils and the status of traditional authorities under current law; the decentralisation description is general.

Draft for teacher review: content is general and non-political; legal ages, institutions, names of laws and any health or road-safety statement must be verified (by a teacher, and for health topics by a health worker) before release.

blocks.md: A country is governed at several levels: the **national** government, **regional** bodies and **local** government. In Cameroon, **local government** is carried out by **councils** (communes) led by a **mayor** and councillors elected by the people of the area. The councils look after local needs and are closest to the citizens. Besides these elected bodies there are **traditional authorities** such as chiefs, Fons and Lamibe.

blocks.caption: From national to local
blocks.alt: Four layers from the national government to villages and community groups.

blocks.title: Services of a council
blocks.md: Councils help to provide and maintain **local roads**, **markets**, **water points**, **street lighting**, **waste collection**, **primary school buildings** and **health centres**, and keep **civil registers** such as birth, marriage and death records. They also issue some local permits and promote local development, working with the central government under the laws on decentralisation.

blocks.title: Traditional authorities
blocks.md: Chiefs and Fons lead communities according to **customs and traditions**, settle small disputes, keep order, represent the community and help to preserve culture. They work with the administration and councils. They must respect the law and the rights of citizens. Traditional rulers are important for community development and unity.

**Taking part.** Citizens take part in local affairs by voting in council elections, attending community meetings, paying taxes and local levies, joining development associations and common initiative groups, reporting problems (such as broken water taps), and helping with communal work. Councils get their **funds** from local taxes and fees, shares of central taxes, and grants for projects. Money must be used for the public good: citizens are entitled to ask how it is used.

blocks.title: Be careful
blocks.md:
- Traditional authorities and elected councils are different institutions; each has its own role.
- A mayor is elected locally; a chief is chosen under local custom.
- Local services need money: avoid damaging them, and support payment of taxes.

blocks.title: Example 1: who does what?
blocks.statement: A village needs a new water point. Which local body would you ask, and what could the villagers contribute?
steps: The council is responsible for many local water points.
The villagers can help with labour and small contributions.
Dialogue with the chief and the council helps.
blocks.answer: The council (with the chief); villagers give labour and contributions.

blocks.title: Example 2: birth certificate
steps: Civil status registers are kept by councils.
So the council civil status office.

objectives: Explain how nationality is acquired in general terms
Describe important identity documents and their uses
Explain the duty to declare births and protect documents
reviewNotes: Teacher to verify the nationality law, the current identity documents, ages and procedures (late registration, identity card issuance); the lesson is deliberately general and avoids specific legal details.

blocks.md: **Nationality** is the legal link between a person and a state. A person who has the nationality of a country is a **citizen** with rights and duties. Nationality is normally acquired **by birth to a citizen parent**, in some cases **by birth in the country**, by **marriage**, or by **naturalisation** (a legal process for foreigners who fulfil conditions). The exact rules are set by the **nationality law** of each country.

blocks.caption: Common documents
blocks.alt: Two columns of documents for a child and an adult.

blocks.title: Identity documents
blocks.md:
- **Birth certificate**: proves name, date and place of birth and parentage; needed for school, exams and later documents.
- **National identity card**: proves identity and nationality of an adult.
- **Passport**: for travel abroad.
- **School ID card**: shows a pupil's school.
- Other documents: marriage certificate, driving licence and voter's card.

**Why a birth certificate matters.** A child without a birth certificate may find it hard to be registered for national exams, to obtain an identity card or a passport, and to prove nationality. Parents have a **duty to declare births** to the civil status authorities soon after birth. **Late registration** is possible but more complicated. Children have a **right to a name and nationality**.

blocks.title: Be careful
blocks.md:
- Keep documents safe and never lend them or sell them: identity theft and fraud are crimes.
- Never use false documents: forgery is a serious offence.
- Lost documents must be reported and replaced through the proper authorities.

blocks.title: Common mistakes
blocks.md:
- Nationality is not the same as ethnic group or religion.
- A citizen is not only someone who votes: children are citizens too.
- Rules on acquiring nationality differ by country; do not assume the rules of another country apply here.

blocks.title: Example 1: which document?
blocks.statement: A pupil needs to prove her date of birth to register for an exam. Which document is most useful?
steps: Date of birth is recorded at birth.

blocks.title: Example 2: lost document
blocks.statement: A man loses his identity card. What should he do?
steps: He should report the loss to the police.
He should apply for a replacement.
He should not let others use it.
blocks.answer: Report the loss and apply for a replacement.
